governanceNotes: D1 batch 68 (2026-09-26): identity deferred (DIRECTION-INVERSION dominance plus diagnostic-mimicry/comorbidity plus no-identity voice outcomes). The located evidence supports no outgoing catalog edge: (i) anxiety and depression - the 164-patient ILO screening cohort (83 adults, 81 children; PMID 38483372) found elevated anxiety (63%/60%), depression (32%/30%), and PTSD (34%/16%) but explicitly notes most affected patients were formally diagnosed PRIOR to ILO evaluation, and the pediatric psychological-factors literature (PMID 41789306) frames psychological factors as contributing TO vocal cord dysfunction; the forward direction (ILO causing incident anxiety or depression) is unquantified, so no edge is authored despite the reverse-direction signal being well documented (the batch-61 mixed-urinary-incontinence anxiety withhold is the family precedent); (ii) asthma - 68 percent comorbidity in the 137-patient UK national registry (PMID 38296051) is comorbidity-only, and the case literature is dominated by diagnostic mimicry (PVFM mimics asthma and anaphylaxis), which is a guard category rather than an edge; (iii) dysphonia and stridor - episode-level voice and breathing symptoms have NO catalog identities (withheld propositions; the catalog holds aphonia for complete voice loss, which PVFM does not produce); (iv) laryngospasm - the catalog identity exists but is itself a deferred zero-edge identity from batch 52 (direction-inversion, procedure-context, magnitude), and the PVFM-laryngospasm relationship is construct-adjacency rather than a secondary-condition pathway; (v) functional impairment and emergency-department utilization (88 percent attended emergency care; 64 percent impaired functional capacity) are morbidity measures, not secondary conditions. Reopening conditions: (a) a longitudinal ILO cohort quantifying incident anxiety, depression, or PTSD diagnoses after ILO onset with baseline mental-health screening; or (b) addition of dysphonia or stridor identities to the catalog, which would unlock the documented episode-symptom literature.
